In the past, porting was from one machine to another (read: CPU, instruction set, and bus width), not one platform to another (which likely has the same kind of CPU, instruction set, and bus width). They would literally take the program from the original assembly and convert the disassembled binary to the equivalent assembler code to be assembled for the target machine.

Later, when higher level languages started to emerge, they were still mostly idiomatic to their own machine and weren’t able to compile code for a similar language implemented on another machine. It wasn’t until the advent of portable high level languages that you could make minor edits to the source and compiler configs and get a binary compiled that would work on the target machine/platform.

On top of that, game developers have to add extra options into PC ports that aren't necessary for consoles. For example, consoles use just one set of hardware, but two different PCs could have completely different GPUs and CPUs. This means that a PC version of a game needs adjustable graphics settings in order look good, unlike most console games. On top of that, a PC version almost always needs re-bindable controls, because who know what input the user has. One user might be using a mouse and keyboard, another might be using a 60% keyboard, and another might use a controller.
